rejected.title: Cultural tourism
card: Cultural tourism is travel to learn about a people's culture. In First Nations-run cultural tourism, a First Nations community or business runs the experience.
Visitors might join a guided walk on Country, an art workshop or a storytelling session. Country is the land, waters and living things a First Nations group belongs to.
The community sets the terms: which stories and knowledge are shared, who shares them and which places visitors may enter. Some stories and sites are kept private.
This brings income and jobs to the community, while it keeps control of its own culture.
rejected.remember: Visitors pay to learn, and the community decides what is shared and how.

a.q: In First Nations-run cultural tourism, who decides which stories are shared with visitors?
opts: The community whose stories they are
The visitors who pay for the tour
The travel agent who sells the tour
The government agency that runs parks
a.why: The community whose stories they are decides what is shared, who shares it and where visitors go. Visitors pay for the experience, but paying does not give them that choice.
a.clue: Think about who the stories belong to.

b.q: Elders of a community in the Kimberley take visitors to a rock art site, but tell them that one nearby place is closed to visitors. What does this show about First Nations-run cultural tourism?
opts: The community sets the terms of each visit
Visitors can choose which places they enter
The closed place has nothing worth seeing
The tour sells goods, not an experience
b.why: The Elders decide which places visitors may enter, so the community is setting the terms of the visit. Keeping a place private does not mean it holds nothing worth seeing: some sites are kept private on purpose.
b.clue: Who made the choice about the closed place?

version.title: Cultural tourism
card: Cultural tourism is travel to learn about a people's culture. First Nations-run cultural tourism is owned or led by First Nations people, who guide the visit.
Visitors might join a walk on Country, an art session or a night of storytelling. Country means the land, waters and living things a First Nations group belongs to.
The community sets the terms: which stories and knowledge are shared, who shares them, where visitors may go and what they may photograph. Some knowledge can be kept private.
The business earns income and creates jobs, often for local people, while the community keeps control of its culture.
version.remember: Visitors pay for the experience, and the community decides what is shared.

a.q: Which is a sign that a cultural tour is run on the community's terms?
opts: Elders choose which stories are shared
Visitors pick any site they want to see
A tour company abroad writes the script
Guides tell every story the group holds
a.why: On the community's terms means the community decides what is shared, who shares it and where visitors go, so Elders choosing the stories fits. Telling every story does not, because the community can keep some knowledge private.
a.clue: Who makes the choices on the tour?

b.q: A First Nations community near Cairns runs a cultural tour business. A large travel company offers to pay more if guides share a private story and let visitors film a ceremony site. What fits First Nations-run cultural tourism?
opts: It can say no, as the community sets the terms
It agrees, since the paying customer sets the terms
It agrees, since more income matters most of all
The company films anyway, since the site is public
b.why: In First Nations-run cultural tourism the community sets the terms, including what is shared and what may be filmed, so it can turn the offer down. Income matters to the business, but paying more does not hand control of the culture to the customer.
b.clue: Who sets the terms of the visit?

a.best: Elders choose which stories are shared

b.best: It can say no, as the community sets the terms
